lesson.title: Your Brain's Alertness Dial
lesson.summary: The reticular activating system is a network of neurons running through the brainstem that regulates arousal and wakefulness by filtering incoming stimuli and controlling how much sensory information reaches conscious awareness.
lesson.body:
Running diffusely through the core of the brainstem, extending up from the medulla through the pons and into the midbrain, is a network of neurons called the reticular formation. Embedded within it is the reticular activating system, the portion of that network most directly responsible for regulating arousal and wakefulness. Rather than processing one specific type of sensory information the way a sensory neuron pathway does, the reticular activating system's job is to control the overall level of alertness of the brain as a whole.

It does this partly by filtering. Enormous amounts of sensory information stream into the brainstem constantly, far more than the cortex could usefully process at once, and the reticular activating system helps determine which of that information is important enough to be passed along and amplified toward conscious awareness, and which can be safely ignored or suppressed. In effect, it acts as a gatekeeper, deciding not what you sense, but how much of what you sense actually reaches the level of conscious attention.

This gatekeeping function is what makes the reticular activating system essential to consciousness itself. The cerebral cortex, where higher-level thought and awareness occur, depends on a steady stream of activating input from the reticular activating system to stay in an alert, wakeful state. When that input decreases, as it does naturally at night, the brain transitions toward sleep. When it is severely disrupted by injury or disease, the result can be coma, since the cortex can be entirely intact and still fail to produce consciousness without sufficient arousal signals arriving from below.

A familiar example of the filtering function is the way a sleeping parent can startle awake at the faint sound of a baby crying in another room while sleeping straight through louder, more constant background noise like traffic outside. The reticular activating system is effectively tuned to treat certain stimuli as meaningful enough to trigger arousal while filtering out others as safe to ignore, even during sleep. Its central role in consciousness is also why general anesthesia works in part by suppressing reticular activating system function, deliberately reducing the arousal signal that would otherwise keep the cortex awake and responsive. In the other direction, stimulant substances such as caffeine promote wakefulness in part by increasing overall arousal, consistent with the reticular activating system's role as the brain's master switch for alertness.

Because the reticular activating system runs directly through the medulla and the rest of the brainstem, damage to that region can impair arousal along with the vital functions discussed earlier. Its arousal signals do not go straight to the cortex, however, they are relayed through the thalamus, the structure covered later in this unit, which helps distribute that activation broadly across the cerebral hemispheres.
